newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Helicopter is secret weapon in Madagascar poll.
newsitem.headline: Helicopter is secret weapon in Madagascar poll.

text.p: A dynamic U.S.-trained millionaire with a secret weapon is shaking up the campaign for Madagascar's presidential elections on Sunday.

Herizo Razafimahaleo is the only candidate with a helicopter, allowing him to dash around the vast island pulling in crowds of mainly young people. The other 14 candidates bounce along pot-holed roads by car.
Razafimahaleo, a 40-year-old businessman, started as a rank outsider in what looked like a three-horse race between Madagascar's two former presidents and its current interim head of state.
But his aggressive campaigning and his pledge to donate the presidential salary to creating jobs for unemployed youths are starting to rattle established politicians.

With the vote likely to be sharply split, the chances of no candidate polling more than 50 percent appear high. In that case a second round run-off between the two top men will be held at a date yet to be announced.
Madagascar has lurched from one political crisis to another since 1993 when a long and bloody battle for democracy ended in triumph and high hopes.

The squabbling has frustrated plans to improve life for the 14 million islanders, among the poorest people in the world. It came to a head when former president Albert Zafy was impeached by parliament last July and the high constitutional court endorsed the decision in September, ordering early elections.

Zafy, aged in his late 60s and known for his trade-mark straw hat, is a leading candidate on Sunday. So are the former military ruler he defeated in 1993, Didier Ratsiraka, and the current prime minister and interim president, Norbert Ratsirahonana.
General Marcel Ranjeva, the armed forces minister, went on state radio on Monday and said security forces would ensure a fair vote.
"We are totally independent of the 15 candidates in competition and we will not accept any deviation from legality.
"Nor is there any possibility that we will take power," Ranjeva said, reading a joint statement also signed by the interior minister and the heads of the police and paramilitary gendarmerie.

Retired admiral Ratsiraka, 59, returned from 19 months of voluntary exile in France at the end of September. His bid to stage a comeback got a boost last weekend when he drew the largest crowd of the campaign in a rally in the capital.
But the violence of the two years in the early 90s when he used the army to resist the pro-democracy movement is coming back to haunt him.

The blackest day in those turbulent years was August 10, 1991, when Ratsiraka ordered troops to fire on a huge crowd of protesters surging towards the presidential palace. Fourteen people were killed and hundreds wounded.
